## Claude synthesis

### Overall Assessment: Useful with Caveats

This paper introduces CICF, a CBAM-derived toolkit for monitoring curriculum implementation — a curriculum-agnostic teacher/leader survey plus five curriculum-specific classroom observation rubrics ("Implementation Progressions") co-designed with the developers of EL Education, Wit & Wisdom, Eureka Math2, Illustrative Mathematics, and OpenSciEd — and reports a two-round field test in 104 schools across 10 states. What it establishes is narrower than its abstract claims. It shows that the instruments can be administered at low cost (median 15 minutes for the survey, 37.5 minutes per observation); that the survey's four focus-area subscales (Unconcerned, Self, Task, Impact) hold together on an independent second-round sample with acceptable-but-not-strong CFA fit (RMSEA .069, CFI .942, TLI .92) and alphas of .78–.96; and that trained observers reach moderate-to-strong agreement on the curriculum-specific rubrics (kappa .60–.85, under a ±0.5-point tolerance, on 14–59 paired observations per curriculum). The field should treat it as the best available public evidence that curriculum-specific implementation rubrics can be built and scored consistently by practitioners — as the abstract's own final sentence puts it, a "promising tool." It should not treat the paper as establishing that CICF is "valid" or "useful" in any stronger sense: content validity rests on unanimous endorsement from the co-designers, usefulness on six self-selected partner leaders, the survey–observation correlations are r ≈ .16, the paper's own Impact hypothesis fails in Table 5 and vanishes from the Discussion and abstract, the Conclusion asserts a link to HQIM "effectiveness" that the Limitations section disclaims, and the sample sizes cannot be reconciled across Tables 2, 4, 5, and 6. The authors are the instrument's developers evaluating their own product and declare no conflicts. Cite the paper for the tools, the design logic, and the burden and reliability numbers with their caveats attached; verify anything else — starting with the ICPSR deposit and the availability of the rubrics themselves — before building on it.

#### Key Strengths

- It fills a real, specific gap. Existing practitioner tools for curriculum implementation are either curriculum-agnostic observation rubrics or self-report surveys; research-grade fidelity instruments are study-specific and training-intensive. Curriculum-specific quality progressions for five of the most widely adopted HQIM, usable by school and system staff in under 40 minutes, did not previously exist in the public literature, and two of the developers are replacing their own observation tools with them.
- The instrument-development architecture is sound: an exploratory Round 1 (EFA, item revision) followed by a confirmatory Round 2 (CFA on a substantially new sample); validity evidence organized under the Standards' five sources and Kane's argument-based framework; inter-rater reliability computed separately for each of the five rubrics rather than pooled; and a principled refusal to run CFA on criterion-referenced rubrics. Table 4's mapping of data source, n, and analytic approach to each research question is unusually transparent and is what makes the cross-checks in this review possible.
- The reliability and feasibility numbers are concrete and, with their footnotes, usable: per-curriculum n, percent agreement, kappa, tau-b, and rho in Table 6, with disclosure of which rounds are pooled and of the ±0.5 tolerance rule; alphas for all four focus-area subscales; and median administration times from a large embedded usability sample. The Findings also state plainly, rather than hiding, that the Impact correlations ran opposite to hypothesis.
- The paper is clean to navigate and reasonably honest at the margins: four research questions carried in the same order through Methods, Findings, and Discussion; a Limitations section that names the two biggest absences (no predictive validity, no test-retest reliability) and concedes small per-analysis samples; an Open Practices statement with an ICPSR/AERA deposit URL; the survey in supplemental materials; and named software (Stata 19).

#### Key Concerns

- Sample sizes cannot be reconciled and the unit of analysis is never fixed. Table 2 sums to 595 survey records and 537 observations; the prose and Table 5 use 582; Table 4 uses 807 for internal consistency and 937 for usability; the CFA n of 240 exceeds Round 2's 217; Table 4's inter-rater n of 212 (identical to Table 2's survey-and-observation 'Both' column) conflicts with Table 6's per-curriculum n's summing to 154; Table 5's IP-score n of 549 exceeds Table 2's 537; Table 3's n column is empty. Units are teacher-curriculum-round combinations, teachers recur across rounds, nothing is clustered, and the number of distinct people is never reported.
- The abstract, Discussion, and Conclusion outrun the findings. The abstract claims 'strong content and construct validity' while the relations-to-other-variables evidence is near-null (survey–observation r = .16) and the Impact hypothesis fails on all three criteria (−.10, −.28, −.15); both facts are conceded in one clause of the Findings and then disappear from the Discussion summary and abstract. The Conclusion says CICF yields data 'to understand variability in the effectiveness of new HQIM' when no outcome data were collected and the Limitations section says predictive validity was not addressed. The abstract's 'meaningful distributions' claim rests on a cross-reference to a descriptive summary that does not exist in the paper.
- The evidence is not independent of the product. CPRL developed CICF, four of five authors are at CPRL, the rubrics were co-designed with the curriculum publishers, and those same publishers and providers served as the content-validity experts (10 of 10 agreed); usefulness rests on six self-selected partner leaders with unanimous top-box responses; the paper reports developers embedding the tools in their commercial offerings; and the conflict-of-interest declaration reads 'none.' None of this is disqualifying for a first field test, but it means the content-validity and usefulness strands carry little independent evidentiary weight, and the paper does not say so.
- The reliability claim is mislabeled and under-specified. 'Substantial agreement' is Landis and Koch's vocabulary, but the paper attributes it to McHugh (2012), whose own table calls .60–.79 'moderate' and .40–.59 'weak' — under which Illustrative Mathematics (kappa .596, the largest sample) is weak. The Methods define agreement as within ±1 point while Table 6's note says ±0.5 on an averaged score; exact agreement, kappa confidence intervals, and any distribution of Implementation Progression scores (which would reveal range restriction) are never reported; three of five rubrics rest on 14–25 pairs; and the rubrics were revised again after the field test, so the validated versions are not the circulated ones.
- Key inputs are missing or unavailable. Only the survey is in the supplement — the five observation rubrics, the paper's distinctive contribution, are never said to be public, and their absorption into publishers' service offerings may constrain access. No code is mentioned. Several promised analyses are absent (chi-square and df for the CFA; alphas for the extent-of-use and feelings scales; the 'consequences of use' validity strand; EFA extraction, rotation, and item-drop rules; the identity of the three low-loading items), and the literature review omits the observation-validation canon (MET, Hill, Charalambous & Kraft 2012, G-theory), the fidelity-measurement canon (Century et al. 2010), and the SoCQ psychometric work that already found CBAM's stages collapse to roughly this four-factor shape.

#### What to Rely On

- The existence, design logic, and component structure of CICF: three dimensions (feelings, extent of use, observed quality of use), four focus areas adapted from CBAM's Stages of Concern (Unconcerned, Self, Task, Impact), a curriculum-agnostic teacher and leader survey, and five curriculum-specific Implementation Progression rubrics co-designed with the developers of EL Education, Wit & Wisdom, Eureka Math2, Illustrative Mathematics, and OpenSciEd.
- Administration burden: a median of 15 minutes to complete the survey and 37.5 minutes per classroom observation, from an embedded usability survey with a large denominator (Table 4 lists n = 937). These are the paper's most planning-useful numbers.
- That trained school- and system-based observers can apply curriculum-specific implementation rubrics with moderate-to-strong tolerance-band agreement — best documented for EL Education (n = 40, kappa .63) and Illustrative Mathematics (n = 59, kappa .60), with higher but less precisely estimated agreement for Eureka Math2 (n = 25), Wit & Wisdom (n = 16), and OpenSciEd (n = 14). Quote Table 6's per-curriculum n's and the ±0.5 weighting rule with any citation.
- That the focus-area survey scale exhibits a four-factor structure on an independent second-round sample with acceptable fit (RMSEA .069, CFI .942, TLI .92; n = 240 as reported) and subscale alphas of .78 (Self), .85 (Unconcerned), .80 (Task), and .96 (Impact). Cite the numbers rather than the abstract's 'strong construct validity' label, and note that this replicates a collapsed structure already found in the SoCQ literature.
- A demand signal from co-design partners: field-test systems requested continued use, and two of the participating curriculum developers began replacing their own observation tools with the Implementation Progressions. Frame this as partner uptake, not as independent evidence of instrument quality.
- The paper's own stated limitations: no predictive validity against student learning, no test-retest reliability, and small samples for several curriculum-specific and feasibility analyses.

#### What to Treat Cautiously

- 'Feasible, useful, and valid, with strong content and construct validity' (abstract) — content validity is unanimous endorsement by the people who co-designed the instruments; usefulness is six self-selected partner leaders; the CFA fit is acceptable under the older .90/.08 conventions but not under Hu & Bentler's; and the relations-to-other-variables strand partly disconfirms the framework.
- '582 teachers and school-level leaders in 104 schools across 10 states' — 582 is the maximum pairwise n in Table 5, not a participant count; units are teacher-curriculum-round combinations, teachers recur across rounds, and the number of distinct individuals is never reported. Every other n in the paper (595, 807, 937, 240, 220, 212, 154, 549, 537) fails to reconcile with it.
- 'Substantial agreement' / 'approximately 80% agreement' among raters — the label is misattributed to McHugh (2012), under whose scale two of five rubrics are 'moderate' or 'weak'; agreement is tolerance-weighted (±0.5 on an averaged score, or ±1 per the Methods), exact agreement is never reported, no confidence intervals are given, three rubrics rest on 14–25 pairs, and the rubrics were revised after the field test.
- Treating the survey and the observation rubrics as two measures of one coherent construct, or using the survey as a low-cost proxy for observed implementation quality — the survey–observation correlations are .16 (extent of use), .16 (feelings), and −.04 to −.15 (focus areas), reported without significance tests or confidence intervals and without clustering.
- The Impact subscale as an indicator of advanced, student-outcome-oriented implementation — it correlates negatively with extent of use (−.10), feelings (−.28), and observed quality (−.15), the reverse of the authors' hypothesis; it was the most heavily revised subscale after the EFA; and its alpha of .96 signals item redundancy. A leader reading a high Impact score as a marker of mature implementation would be reading it backwards relative to Table 5.
- The Conclusion's claim that CICF provides data 'to understand variability in the effectiveness of new HQIM' and the Implications' claim that CICF 'can be used to support HQIM implementation' — no student-outcome, comparison-group, or pre-post data exist in the study, and the Limitations section says predictive validity was not addressed.
- The abstract's 'useful variation and meaningful distributions' — the supporting sentence cross-references a summary of descriptive statistics that does not appear in the paper; no item means, SDs, response distributions, or Implementation Progression score distributions are reported anywhere, and Figure 2 carries no scale, direction, or n.
- The paper's account of the HQIM-effects literature — Blazar et al. (2019) is cited three times as supportive when its headline result is null; Kane et al. (2016) is a perceptions study, not an achievement estimate; Quinn & Kim (2017) is a randomized experiment whose finding partly cuts against the paper's fidelity framing; cost-effectiveness claims rest entirely on think-tank briefs; 'Grunow & Park, 2024' has no reference-list entry. Verify against primary sources before repeating.
- Generalization beyond the five named curricula, beyond K–8 (1% of the sample taught grades 9–12), beyond volunteer partner systems, and beyond observers normed and given feedback by the research team — the rubrics are curriculum-specific by construction, and reliability under routine district norming was not tested.
- The reproducibility of any headline statistic from the article alone — the CFA's chi-square, df, item list, and loadings table are missing; the EFA is undocumented; composite construction and the combination of two observers' ratings into one score are unstated; no code is mentioned; and the observation rubrics are not said to be available. Check the ICPSR/AERA deposit for what it actually contains before relying on the numbers.

## Codex synthesis

### Overall Assessment: Useful With Caveats

Shand and colleagues provide useful preliminary evidence for the Curriculum Implementation Change Framework (CICF), a curriculum-focused adaptation of the Concerns-Based Adoption Model that combines educator surveys, curriculum-specific observation rubrics, and support for interpreting implementation data. The published study documents practitioner acceptability under research-team support, expert judgments of content alignment, an encouraging survey factor model, and curriculum-specific observer agreement (pp. 6–13; Figure 1; Table 6). It does not establish that using CICF improves instruction or student learning, or that its scores support comparisons across settings or over time (pp. 9, 13–14). My judgment is that the applied contribution merits selective citation and further formative use, while the broad validation claim requires qualification: survey–observation associations are modest, the meaning of the Impact construct remains unsettled, and unresolved sample and scoring documentation limits independent assessment (Tables 2, 4–6, pp. 6–7, 12–13). The adequate methods and contribution assessments and the weak writing and reproducibility assessments are compatible: the field test offers real evidence, but its reporting does not support unrestricted confidence in the toolkit's intended uses.

#### Key Strengths

- The contribution is concrete and its lineage is explicit: CICF adapts CBAM to curriculum implementation and combines educator perspectives with curriculum-aligned observations and dashboards (pp. 2–5; Table 1, p. 5). Its principal value is practical measurement development; comparative superiority over existing tools is not tested.
- The validation strategy draws on expert review, response-process evidence, iterative instrument revision, survey factor analysis, and paired observations, with research questions mapped to evidence sources (Table 4, p. 7; pp. 8–11). This is an appropriate foundation for an initial instrument-development study.
- The reported observation results offer encouraging evidence of consistency under the field-test conditions: curriculum-specific Cohen's kappa values range from 0.596 to 0.849 under the table's tolerance-based agreement convention (Table 6 and its note, p. 13). These are reported coefficients verified against the PDF, not independently reestimated results.
- Participating leaders describe ways the information informed professional-learning discussions and exposed implementation concerns (p. 10). These accounts illustrate plausible formative uses, although their effectiveness was not independently evaluated.
- The article acknowledges unexpected Impact relationships and untested predictive validity and test–retest reliability (p. 11; Table 5, p. 12; p. 13), and provides a versioned data-repository link (Open Practices, p. 14). Those disclosures help readers identify both the study's limits and a potential replication route.

#### Key Concerns

- Broad validation is premature. The CFA addresses the survey focus statements, not the observation rubrics (p. 9; Figure 1, p. 11). Observed implementation correlates only 0.16 with each of reported use and feelings, while Impact correlates −0.15 with observed implementation and −0.28 with feelings (Table 5, p. 12). These document limited convergence and unexpected directions; my judgment is that they constrain a unified developmental interpretation without automatically invalidating distinct measures.
- Core reporting and replication details remain unresolved. Table 2 reports Round 2 survey totals of '202' teachers and '15' school leaders (p. 6), whereas Table 4 reports '240' for 'Round 2 survey (revised focus areas)' (p. 7). The methods define agreement as 'within one point of each other (exact and adjacent agreement)' (p. 9), whereas Table 6 says 'Weighted so that ±0.5 points on the average scale counts as agreement' (p. 13). These are verified differences without a documented reconciliation, not established computational errors. Complete instruments and online supplements are not bound into the PDF and were unavailable; the stated repository's contents could not be verified.
- The construct relationships need explanation: Self–Impact is labeled '−.19' in the latent-factor diagram (Figure 1, p. 11) and '.37' in the observed-score correlation table (Table 5, p. 12). These are different estimands and may use different samples or scoring, so the opposing signs do not prove either exhibit is wrong. The paper does not explain their relationship, limiting confidence in a simple interpretation of the focus areas.
- Feasibility and usefulness were assessed in supported participating settings, with overlapping participation across administrations, limited recruitment information, and incompletely specified handling of repeated records and school dependence (pp. 5–10). Transfer to routine unsupported use, score comparability across populations, longitudinal interpretation, and effects on teaching or learning remain unestablished (p. 13). These are limits on inference, not evidence that the tools cannot work.
- The literature establishes a plausible rationale but does not demonstrate an exhaustive practical gap or comparative advantage (pp. 2–5). Its treatment of adaptation on p. 3 underplays the conditional benefits reported by the cited Quinn and Kim experiment, and its account of curriculum effects gives limited attention to the null differences summarized by the cited Blazar research team. My judgment is that readers should consult those sources before using this article as a synthesis of effectiveness or fidelity evidence. [Quinn and Kim, abstract, p. 1187](https://files.eric.ed.gov/fulltext/EJ1162351.pdf); [Learning by the Book, study overview](https://cepr.harvard.edu/curriculum).

#### What to Rely On

- CICF is a documented CBAM-informed approach to combining educator perceptions and curriculum-specific observations—cite the paper for its design, adaptation, and initial field testing (pp. 2–9; Table 1, p. 5).
- The tested survey focus statements have preliminary support from expert feedback and their fitted internal structure—cite this as component-specific evidence, retaining the weaker indicators and planned revisions discussed with Figure 1 (pp. 10–11).
- Trained observers achieved the curriculum-specific agreement reported in Table 6—attach its tolerance rule and instrument-round restrictions whenever citing these reliability results (p. 13, Table 6 and note).
- Participating leaders reported that CICF information was useful for discussing and planning implementation support—attribute this to supported users' experiences, rather than treating it as measured improvement in decisions or outcomes (p. 10).

#### What to Treat Cautiously

- Claims that the entire toolkit is generally validated or interchangeable across curricula, roles, and settings require further evidence—component-specific CFA and agreement results do not establish measurement equivalence, predictive accuracy, or longitudinal stability (p. 9; Figure 1, p. 11; Table 6 and Limitations, p. 13).
- Claims that positive feelings or greater self-reported use reliably identify better observed implementation need qualification—the relevant correlations are each 0.16, and the study reports associations rather than causal effects (Table 5, p. 12).
- Precise sample-size, agreement, and focus-area claims should be checked against the relevant analysis and instrument version—the quoted count, scoring-rule, and latent-versus-observed differences above remain unresolved (Tables 2, 4–6, pp. 6–7, 12–13; Figure 1, p. 11).
- Claims that CICF improves instruction, saves resources, raises achievement, or explains curriculum effectiveness exceed this field test—testimonials and proposed applications do not establish those effects, and student-outcome validation remains future work (pp. 10, 13–14).
- Using scores to rank teachers, compare curricula, or interpret individual change requires evidence beyond this study—classification accuracy, cross-group comparability, and stability over time are not established (pp. 9, 13).
- Claims of theoretical priority, superiority to existing tools, or a general preference for fidelity over adaptation should not rest on this paper—the framework explicitly extends CBAM, lacks a head-to-head comparison, and presents the adaptation literature selectively (pp. 2–5; [Quinn and Kim, abstract, p. 1187](https://files.eric.ed.gov/fulltext/EJ1162351.pdf)).

#### Verification notes

- CONFIRMED — Methods, writing, and reproducibility reviews: Table 2's Round 2 survey totals are '202' teachers and '15' leaders (p. 6), while Table 4's 'Round 2 survey (revised focus areas)' is '240' (p. 7); the paper supplies no reconciliation.
- CONFIRMED — Methods and contribution reviews: use–observation and feelings–observation correlations are each 0.16; Impact–observation is −0.15 and Impact–feelings is −0.28 (Table 5, p. 12).
- CONFIRMED — Methods and writing reviews: Self–Impact is '−.19' in Figure 1 (p. 11) versus '.37' in Table 5 (p. 12); this is an unexplained latent-versus-observed difference, not a verified calculation error.
- CONFIRMED — Agreement reviews: kappa ranges from 0.596 to 0.849, with percent agreement from 76% to 93% (Table 6, p. 13); 'within one point' in the methods (p. 9) and '±0.5 points on the average scale' in the table note (p. 13) are not reconciled.
- CONFIRMED — Methods, writing, and contribution reviews: the CFA is limited to survey focus statements (p. 9; Figure 1, p. 11), and the limitations explicitly leave predictive validity and test–retest reliability untested (p. 13).
- CONFIRMED — Literature review: the paper's adaptation-risk discussion (p. 3) omits the conditional benefit in [Quinn and Kim's abstract, p. 1187](https://files.eric.ed.gov/fulltext/EJ1162351.pdf); the [Blazar team's study overview](https://cepr.harvard.edu/curriculum) reports little evidence of average achievement-growth differences across textbooks.
- CONFIRMED — Literature review: the blanket shared-stage description on p. 3 does not accurately characterize the cited [Wandersman et al. abstract](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1007/s10464-008-9174-z), which organizes the framework around interacting synthesis/translation, support, and delivery systems.
- COULD NOT CHECK — Reproducibility review: the versioned [ICPSR deposit](https://www.icpsr.umich.edu/sites/aera/view/studies/306864/versions/V1.0) is explicitly linked on p. 14, but retrieval failed; data, code, codebooks, and instrument-version completeness remain unverified, and online supplements are unavailable under this review's conditions.

## Responses

Authors of the reviewed paper, and readers who find an error in a review, can respond in the discussion thread below (it needs a GitHub account), or open an issue in the site's GitHub repository. Corrections are logged on the Corrections page with dates.
